newsitem.title: UK: UK-Asia aircargo volumes good but rates pressured.
newsitem.headline: UK-Asia aircargo volumes good but rates pressured.

text.p: Ex-UK to Asia airfreight volumes are generally strong at present despite the perceived negative effect on exports of strong sterling, a Reuters survey shows.

But average rates on five of 12 key London-Asia routes have declined since late June as additional bellyhold cargo capacity on extra summer passenger flights has increased competition and downward pressure on prices, observers noted.
Increased summer space availability also helped to cope with cargo affected by last week's cancellation of many British Airways ex-UK flights due to a cabin crew strike.
As a result, the strike had little impact on airfreight flow out of the country.

There is plenty of airfreight moving to Hong Kong after its handover to China by Britain, although rates have fallen, while UK-Japan remains steady and the Korea route continues to show volume expansion after a shaky first half of 1997.

Ex-London to China, Taiwan and Indonesia yields have either improved or are holding firm and the Philippines and Singapore markets are recording healthy performances for some but not all carriers, the survey showed.
Cathay Pacific Airways said that from Britain to Hong Kong, "we are busier now than we expected to be" and that yields were healthy despite sterling's strength.
"This is supposed to be the slack season but this time round it certainly isn't," said Cathay's north UK cargo manager Ivor Llewellyn.

He felt the main reason was that UK producers, which used to shut down for two or three entire weeks in July/August, were now tending to stagger these close-down periods, or otherwise remain operating.
But Thai Airways International is worried that rates are so low it may not be worth the effort to compete on the now more open UK-HK market, said UK cargo manager Mike Miller.

Airlanka has no fears about London-HK, which it serves via Colombo. "Since the handover weekend, our business has been booming on the route and I foresee this continuing," said the carrier's UK cargo manager Ken Dourado.
The London-Japan market was "a bit slower than we expected" in January-March, said All Nippon Airways' assistant UK cargo manager John O'Shea.
"Because of the strong pound, the number of quotes we are doing is down while we are also seeing some shipments move to (cheaper) seafreight, especially garments" he said.
"We see the next quarter as quite flat but are hopeful of a revival in October-November," stated O'Shea, who reported more spot rating was underway than usual at this time of the year.
Cathay said that ex-UK demand for Japan had eased off recently, even though the UK station had been getting increasing space allocations because of soft Hong Kong-Japan conditions.
But Korean Air (KAL) UK cargo sales manager Frank Smith said his Japan business was recovering and pointed to strong demand for computer equipment from Ireland.
He said the UK-Seoul market "has suddenly come alive" since mid-June, although admitted that rates had softened.

"We have gone from famine to feast," he said, adding that while sterling's strength did not appear to be curtailing exports at present, KAL was nevertheless still 20 percent below its UK target for the year, while Germany was above.
"The Korean government seems to have stopped discouraging imports, especially in the consumer field," he said.
Cathay described its London-Seoul business as steady and said it had space available to sell from the UK which was previously reserved by Hong Kong.
Demand for UK-China airfreight services is spasmodic, said Ashraf Salama, of China Eastern's UK cargo agent, Jet Link.
KAL's Smith said that ex-London to north-east China business had not been good, but quite a lot of enquiries were being received for Shanghai.
"There is also a lot of demand for telecommunications equipment shipments to south China," he said.

Taiwan is "fairly strong and steady for us and has been for some while", said Cathay's Llewellyn, while Thai Airways reported it was doing well ex-London to the carrier's new Indonesian destination of Surabaya, carrying mainly oil industry equipment and ships' spares.
Philippine Airlines' PAL.CN UK cargo department has been told it can fly virtually no freight to Manila between July-September.

The reason, explained UK cargo manager Keith O'Callaghan, is that the onset of Manila's monsoon season has meant that PAL's normally used, nearby Clark alternative landing airport, has had to be substituted by a gateway further away from the storm clouds -- Cebu.
"More fuel therefore has to be loaded in London for the extra 70 minutes' flight-time for our four weekly A340 flights and that means zero cargo, he said.
Unsurprisingly, other carriers have leapt in to cater for the demand.

"We are getting some good ex-UK loads to Manila, via Doha. We have just operated an A300-600 passenger flight on the route carrying 15 tonnes of bottletops," said Qatar Airways' UK cargo manager John Curd.
KAL is also doing well from London to Manila. "We are getting strong demand for telecoms equipment and are moving 14-tonne loads," said Smith.
Singapore Airlines' ex-UK business to Singapore is "excellent", said UK cargo manager Barry Gibson. "I can't believe how well we are doing to this and all of our destinations," he added.
"The strength of sterling seems to be having no impact and perhaps this may not be seen until end-1997 or early-98," he said.
Gibson added he was sticking to his published rates and yields were being maintained.
Airlanka's Dourado said that for him, the Singapore market was "reasonably healthy despite all the competition".
Thailand's de facto devaluation of the baht in early July has had no immediate effect on UK-Bangkok airfreight trading and any impact will take about three months to assess, said Thai's Miller.

"The market is quite strong. Obviously, the baht's devaluation coupled with strong sterling makes it even more expensive for Thai importers to buy British goods. But I don't see the latest events having much effect on our business. I am confident about the future," he said

Airlines report widely differing UK-Australia air cargo performances over recent weeks, with Thai saying that its business on the route declined 20 percent over the past three months compared with the same period last year.
"It has always been a fluctuating market. It is down now but I'm sure it will pick up again," said Miller.
In contrast, Cathay's Lewellyn said the route was presently "buoyant" with its limited through UK-Sydney capacity available fully booked a week in advance.
SIA also said UK-Australia business was "excellent" and space at a premium.
KAL said it had been achieving "quite a bit of success" moving machinery from Britain to Australia and added that demand had picked up to New Zealand.
To South Asia, Airlanka said it was filling its 13 tonnes' cargo capacity on four weekly Heathrow-Colombo A340 flights, with 60 percent offloaded at Sri Lanka and the rest transported onward.
"To Colombo, we are doing particularly well carrying generators, machinery parts and motor spares, plus some fabrics," said Ken Dourado.
As for the Middle East, rates to Dubai and Abu Dhabi are particularly low at present," said Qatar Airways' Curd.
"BA is offering ridiculously low pallet rates to Dubai and the presence of charter operators also keeps prices down. So we tend not to compete in this market," he stated.
Instead, he said, ex-Heathrow Qatar Air was concentrating on selling Doha and onward connections to Dhahran, Jeddah, Kuwait and Muscat, which produced high yields.
